items.title: Complex Polynomials as a Product of Linear Factors

blocks.text: The book prints this heading as “1.2 Complex Polynomials as a Product of Linear Factors”.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The number 1.2 is printed a second time: it was already used for “1.2 Equality of Two Complex Numbers”. In the book's order this section would be 1.3 (its next sub-heading is printed 1.3.1). The printed title is kept here without the number.
A complex polynomial \(P(z)\) is a polynomial function of the complex variable \(z\) with complex coefficients. It is expressed in the general form as

blocks.text_alt: P of z equals a n z to the power n plus a n minus 1 z to the power n minus 1 plus and so on plus a 1 z plus a 0

blocks.text: where \(a_{n}, a_{n-1}, \dots, a_{1}, a_{0}\) are complex numbers (\(a_{n} \ne 0\)), and \(n \ge 0\) is an integer representing the degree of the polynomial.

For example, \(P_{1}(z) = (1 - i)z + 3i\), \(P_{2}(z) = (5 - 4i)z^{2} + (2 + i)z + (3 - 4i)\) and \(P_{3}(z) = (2 - i)z^{3} + 2z^{2}i + (5 + 3i)\) are examples of linear, quadratic and cubic complex polynomials respectively. If \(n = 0\), then \(P(z)\) becomes a constant polynomial.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The degree is the highest power of \(z\) that appears: 1 in \(P_{1}\), 2 in \(P_{2}\), 3 in \(P_{3}\). The coefficient of that highest power, \(a_{n}\), is the leading coefficient; it must not be zero, otherwise the degree would be lower. A real polynomial such as \(z^{2} + 4\) is also a complex polynomial, because every real number is a complex number with imaginary part 0.
A fundamental property of complex polynomials is that they can always be factored into a product of linear factors.
According to the Fundamental theorem of algebra, a polynomial of degree \(n \ge 1\) has exactly \(n\) roots in the complex numbers system \(C\).
A corollary to this theorem states that any polynomial \(P(z)\) of degree \(n\) can be factored completely into a constant \(a\) and \(n\) linear factors over \(C\) in the form

blocks.text_alt: P of z equals a times (z minus z 1) times (z minus z 2) and so on up to (z minus z n), equation 1

blocks.text: where \(z_{1}, z_{2}, \dots, z_{n}\) are complex roots of the polynomial. Once we know the roots of a polynomial equation, we can apply equation (1) to factor the polynomial \(P(z)\) into \(n\) linear factors. Specifically, if \(z_{1}\) and \(z_{2}\) are roots of the polynomial equation \(P(z) = 0\), then \(P(z) = (z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A corollary is a result that follows directly from a theorem. The constant \(a\) in (1) is the leading coefficient \(a_{n}\).
So the last statement, \(P(z) = (z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\), is for a quadratic whose leading coefficient is 1. If the leading coefficient is not 1, keep it in front: for example \(2z^{2} - 12z + 50 = 2(z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\) (Example 10).
"Exactly \(n\) roots" counts a repeated root as many times as it repeats: \(z^{2} = 0\) has the root 0 twice.

For example, the polynomial \(P(x) = x^{2} + 4\) with real coefficients has no real roots, so it cannot be factored into linear polynomials with real coefficients. However, if we consider it as a complex polynomial \(P(z) = z^{2} + 4\), it is easily factored into two linear factors:

blocks.text_alt: z squared plus 4 equals (z plus 2 i) times (z minus 2 i)

blocks.text: where \(2i\) and \(-2i\) are the complex roots of \(z^{2} + 4 = 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does this work? \((2i)^{2} = 4i^{2} = -4\), so \(z^{2} + 4 = z^{2} - (2i)^{2}\), a difference of two squares: \(a^{2} - b^{2} = (a + b)(a - b)\). Over the real numbers \(z^{2} + 4\) cannot be split, but over \(C\) it always can.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: If \(P(z)\) is a polynomial function, the values of \(z\) that satisfy \(P(z) = 0\) are called the zeros of the function \(P(z)\) and roots of the polynomial equation \(P(z) = 0\).

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: Factorize the polynomial \(P(z) = z^{2} + (1 - i)z - i\).
steps:
Given: \(P(z) = z^{2} + (1 - i)z - i\).
To find: its linear factors.
Method: open the bracket in the middle term and factorize by grouping (taking a common factor from pairs of terms).

Step 1: Open the bracket
\[P(z) = z^{2} + z - iz - i\]
Why: \((1 - i)z = z - iz\). Now there are four terms that can be grouped in pairs.

Step 2: Take common factors from each pair
\[= z(z + 1) - i(z + 1)\]
Why: \(z\) is common in \(z^{2} + z\), and \(-i\) is common in \(-iz - i\). Both pairs leave the same bracket \(z + 1\).

Step 3: Take \((z + 1)\) common
\[= (z + 1)(z - i)\]
Why: the same bracket appears in both terms, so it is a common factor.

Check:
\[(z + 1)(z - i) = z^{2} - iz + z - i\]
\[= z^{2} + (1 - i)z - i\]
It equals \(P(z)\). The zeros are \(z = -1\) and \(z = i\).

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: \(P(z) = z^{2} - 4iz + 12\).
To find: its linear factors.
Method: split the middle term. We need two numbers whose sum is \(-4i\) and whose product is \(12\). Writing \(12\) as \(-12i^{2}\) shows that \(-6i\) and \(2i\) work.

Step 1: Write \(12\) using \(i^{2}\)
\[P(z) = z^{2} - 4iz - (-12)\]
\[= z^{2} - 4iz - i^{2}12\]
Why: \(i^{2} = -1\), so \(-i^{2}12 = 12\). In this form the constant term contains \(i^{2}\), which makes the two numbers easy to see.

Step 2: Split the middle term
\[= z^{2} - i6z + i2z - i^{2}12\]
Why: \(-6i + 2i = -4i\) (the middle coefficient) and \((-6i)(2i) = -12i^{2} = 12\) (the constant term).

Step 3: Group in pairs
\[= z(z - 6i) + 2i(z - 6i)\]
Why: \(z\) is common in \(z^{2} - 6iz\); \(2i\) is common in \(2iz - 12i^{2}\) because \(2i \cdot 6i = 12i^{2}\).

Step 4: Take \((z - 6i)\) common
\[= (z - 6i)(z + 2i)\]
Why: the bracket is the same in both terms.

Check:
\[(z - 6i)(z + 2i) = z^{2} + 2iz - 6iz - 12i^{2}\]
\[= z^{2} - 4iz + 12\]
It equals \(P(z)\). The zeros are \(z = 6i\) and \(z = -2i\).

blocks.title: Example 8
blocks.problem: Factorize the polynomial \(P(z) = z^{3} + (1 + i)z^{2} + iz\).
steps:
Given: \(P(z) = z^{3} + (1 + i)z^{2} + iz\).
To find: its linear factors.
Method: every term contains \(z\), so first take \(z\) common; the quadratic left over is factorized by grouping.

Step 1: Take \(z\) common
\[P(z) = z[z^{2} + (1 + i)z + i]\]
Why: \(z\) divides every term; this already gives one linear factor, \(z\).

Step 2: Open the bracket
\[= z[z^{2} + z + iz + i]\]
Why: \((1 + i)z = z + iz\), giving four terms to group.

Step 3: Group in pairs
\[= z[z(z + 1) + i(z + 1)]\]
Why: \(z\) is common in \(z^{2} + z\) and \(i\) is common in \(iz + i\).

Step 4: Take \((z + 1)\) common
\[= z[(z + 1)(z + i)]\]
\[= z(z + 1)(z + i)\]
These are the linear factors.
Why: the same bracket appears in both terms.

Check:
\[(z + 1)(z + i) = z^{2} + (1 + i)z + i\]
Multiplying by \(z\) gives \(z^{3} + (1 + i)z^{2} + iz = P(z)\). A cubic has three linear factors, as the theorem says; the zeros are \(0, -1, -i\).

blocks.title: Key Concept
blocks.text:
The Rational Root Theorem is a mathematical tool used to find all possible rational roots of a polynomial equation with integer coefficients. According to the rational root theorem:
If a polynomial \(P(x) = a_{n}x^{n} + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_{1}x + a_{0}\) has integer coefficients, then every rational root \(\frac{p}{q}\) (in simplest terms) satisfies:
(i) \(p\) is a factor of the constant term \(a_{0}\).
(ii) \(q\) is a factor of the leading coefficient \(a_{n}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: How to use it: write all factors of \(a_{0}\) (with \(\pm\)), all factors of \(a_{n}\), form every fraction \(p/q\), and substitute them one by one until \(P = 0\). The theorem only gives candidates; it does not promise that any of them is a root. Once one root \(r\) is found, \(z - r\) is a factor and synthetic division lowers the degree by one.

blocks.title: Example 9
steps:
Given: \(P(z) = z^{3} - 3z^{2} + z + 5\), a cubic with integer coefficients.
To find: its linear factors.
Method: find one root with the Rational Root Theorem, divide by that factor using synthetic division, and solve the remaining quadratic with the quadratic formula.

Step 1: List the possible rational roots
Constant term \(a_{0} = 5\): factors \(p = \pm1, \pm5\). Leading coefficient \(a_{3} = 1\): factors \(q = \pm1\).
\[\frac{p}{q} = \pm1,\ \pm5\]
According to the Rational Root Theorem, the possible roots of the equation are ±1 and ±5.
Why: any rational root \(p/q\) must have \(p\) a factor of 5 and \(q\) a factor of 1.

Step 2: Test the candidates
\[P(1) = 1 - 3 + 1 + 5 = 4 \ne 0\]
\[P(-1) = (-1)^{3} - 3(-1)^{2} + (-1) + 5\]
\[= -1 - 3 - 1 + 5 = 0\]
So \(z = -1\) is a root and \(z + 1\) is a factor of \(P(z)\).
Why: if \(P(a) = 0\) then \(z - a\) is a factor (factor theorem); here \(a = -1\) gives \(z - (-1) = z + 1\).

Step 3: Synthetic division by −1
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrr} -1 & 1 & -3 & 1 & 5 \\ & & -1 & 4 & -5 \\ \hline & 1 & -4 & 5 & 0 \end{array}\]
Bring down 1; \(1 \times (-1) = -1\), \(-3 + (-1) = -4\); \(-4 \times (-1) = 4\), \(1 + 4 = 5\); \(5 \times (-1) = -5\), \(5 + (-5) = 0\).
\[z^{3} - 3z^{2} + z + 5 = (z + 1)(z^{2} - 4z + 5) \ \text{...(i)}\]
Why: the last row gives the coefficients of the quotient \(z^{2} - 4z + 5\); the final 0 is the remainder, confirming that \(z + 1\) is a factor.

Step 4: Solve \(z^{2} - 4z + 5 = 0\) by the quadratic formula
Here \(a = 1,\ b = -4,\ c = 5\).
\[z = \dfrac{-(-4) \pm \sqrt{(-4)^{2} - 4(1)(5)}}{2(1)}\]
\[= \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 20}}{2} = \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{-4}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{4 \pm 2i}{2}\]
The book then prints \(z = 2 \pm 2i\).
Why: \(\sqrt{-4} = \sqrt{4}\sqrt{-1} = 2i\). Dividing both terms of the numerator by 2 must also divide the \(2i\) (see the Book correction after this example).

Step 5: Write the quadratic factors
\[z^{2} - 4z + 5 = (z - (2 + i))(z - (2 - i))\]
\[= (z - 2 - i)(z - 2 + i)\]
Why: by the corollary, a quadratic with leading coefficient 1 and roots \(z_{1}, z_{2}\) equals \((z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\).

Step 6: Substitute in equation (i)
\[z^{3} - 3z^{2} + z + 5\]
\[= (z + 1)(z - 2 - i)(z - 2 + i)\]
Why: replacing the quadratic in (i) by its two linear factors gives three linear factors for the cubic.

Check:
\[(z - 2 - i)(z - 2 + i) = (z - 2)^{2} - i^{2}\]
\[= z^{2} - 4z + 4 + 1 = z^{2} - 4z + 5\]
\[(z + 1)(z^{2} - 4z + 5) = z^{3} - 3z^{2} + z + 5\]
Both products return the original polynomial.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
1. The question prints \u201cFactorize the + polynomial\u201d; the stray \u201c+\u201d should not be there: \u201cFactorize the polynomial \(P(z) = z^{3} - 3z^{2} + z + 5\)\u201d.
2. In the quadratic formula step the book prints \(z = 2 \pm 2i\). Dividing \(4 \pm 2i\) by 2 gives \(z = 2 \pm i\). (With \(2 \pm 2i\) the quadratic would be \(z^{2} - 4z + 8\), not \(z^{2} - 4z + 5\).) The book's next lines already use the correct roots \(2 + i\) and \(2 - i\), so its final factorization \((z + 1)(z - 2 - i)(z - 2 + i)\) is correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A complex polynomial of degree \(n \ge 1\) has exactly \(n\) roots in \(C\) (Fundamental theorem of algebra).
2. Corollary: \(P(z) = a(z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\dots(z - z_{n})\), where \(a\) is the leading coefficient.
3. Zeros of \(P(z)\) = roots of \(P(z) = 0\).
4. Tools: grouping (Examples 6-8), splitting the middle term (Example 7), Rational Root Theorem + synthetic division + quadratic formula (Example 9).
5. Always multiply the factors back to check.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Dropping the leading coefficient \(a\) when writing the factors.
2. Forgetting that \(i^{2} = -1\) when checking: \((z - 6i)(z + 2i)\) contains \(-12i^{2} = +12\).
3. In \(\frac{4 \pm 2i}{2}\), dividing only the 4 by 2: both terms must be divided, giving \(2 \pm i\).
4. A root \(z = a\) gives the factor \(z - a\): the root \(-1\) gives \(z + 1\), not \(z - 1\).
